tldr: We tested whether simple, interpretable measures of how far a variant target is from a detection guide (Cas13a, data from the ADAPT work of Metsky and colleagues) predict how much detection activity is lost, on data the models never saw.

Which positions mismatch matters more than how many: a position-weighted distance beat mismatch count on held-out guides, held-out regions, held-out targets, and the strictest test (guides and targets both unseen).
A k-mer spectrum distance did not help. The gain is real but modest, and it comes from one lab dataset.

Two warnings: at a useful catch rate (90% of failures) most alarms are false (precision about 0.30 against a 13% base rate), and a threshold set on 0 to 3 mismatches stops working at 4 or more (it flags everything). Calibration does not survive that shift.

sections.title: Why this, and what we think it is for
body: Our reading of the Phase 4 brief is a biosecurity use: detection tools have to keep working as pathogens vary. A concrete, narrow version is an escape flag for an existing assay: given a guide whose normal activity is known, does a variant target push it down to background?

This is classification of existing measurements only. No guides, probes or variants were generated or designed, in line with the project guardrails. We did not verify any specific company's requirements; treat the framing as ours.

Starting point was Hayden Metsky's ADAPT and CATCH (both MIT licensed). We could not find a specific, dated Sabeti-lab paper on sequence distance, so 'in line with Sabeti' here means only the general direction of her lab's diagnostics and benchmarking work. The 2025 Cas13a guide-generation paper we found is design work and is out of scope.

sections.title: What exactly was done
body: Data: the Cas13a dataset published with ADAPT (adapt-seq-design, MIT): 85 guides each measured against about 225 targets, about 19,000 measurements, plus negative controls.

Task 1 (distance): predict each pair's activity change relative to that guide's own perfect-match reading. Task 2 (escape flag): call a pair 'failed' when its measured activity is at the measurement floor (log k = -4.0). Every one of the 255 negative controls reads exactly -4.0 and no measurement is lower, so -4.0 is the floor of the assay: 'failed' means indistinguishable from background. 13% of measurements are at the floor.

Three distances of our own, built on the mismatch idea behind ADAPT: (D1) position-weighted mismatches, which learns how much each position in the guide matters; (D2) which substitution it is, plus adjacent mismatch runs; (D3) k-mer spectrum difference between guide and target window. Plain mismatch count is the baseline, and a model of just the guide's own reference activity is a second baseline.

Models are deliberately simple (ridge regression) so the distance, not model capacity, is what is tested. Everything is scored out-of-fold. Uncertainty comes from resampling guides, with paired comparisons against the baselines.

Splits: random pairs (shown only as a leaky reference, because every guide appears about 225 times), held-out guides, held-out position blocks, held-out clusters of overlapping guides (only 3 exist), held-out targets, held-out guides AND targets together (the strict test), and train on 0 to 3 mismatches then test on 4 or more.
The pass rule was written in the script before the first run. After run 1 we made the baseline stricter (see below); that amendment is disclosed in the code, and the first run's output is kept.

sections.title: What failed, was refused, or should not be trusted
body: The k-mer spectrum distance (D3) gave no gain over mismatch count and was slightly worse when extrapolating.

Our first attempt at a 'strict' verdict printed false for everything. That was an artefact: the categorical baseline cannot predict mismatch counts it never saw, so it returns a constant. We kept the printed result and explain it here instead of quietly changing the rule.

Threshold transfer failed. Chosen to catch 90% of failures on 0 to 3 mismatches, the threshold flagged every pair at 4 or more mismatches (recall 1.00, precision equal to the base rate, about 0.30). So a ranking that looks good (AUROC 0.78 to 0.80 there) does not give a usable go or no-go call under that shift.
Precision at 90% recall is only about 0.29 to 0.30 even on easy splits, with a 13% failure base rate. In practice that is many false alarms for each real failure.
The pre-trained ADAPT models cannot be used for this test: they were trained on this same dataset, so scoring them here would flatter them. We did not run ADAPT's own CNN on our splits yet.

A survey of BV-BRC found no usable structured severity labels (the disease field is empty for influenza, rotavirus and rabies; the surveillance severity field is empty), so clinical-severity endpoints are not available from there.
Two web searches on antibody-escape or receptor-binding data and on antiviral-resistance data were refused by a safety filter. We deliberately did not rephrase them, and those endpoints are left out.
Smaller setbacks: the ADAPT environment needed an older protobuf pin; a first count query silently returned totals and was redone with facet queries.

sections.title: Limits
body: One dataset from one library. Targets are engineered and natural variants of a small set of regions, so 'held-out targets' is weaker than it sounds, and our features do not use target identity at all, which is partly why held-out guides and targets change little.
The escape flag assumes the guide's perfect-match activity is known (true for a deployed assay, not for a brand-new guide).
Everything is in silico on existing measurements. Nothing was validated in a lab.
The failure label sits at an instrument floor, so 'failed' means 'not distinguishable from background in this assay', not 'would miss a patient sample'.

sections.title: Next steps
body: Retrain ADAPT's own model on the same splits as a fair comparison (CPU, small).
Test on a second, independent dataset with natural viral diversity, and on whole held-out viruses. This is the test that matters most.
Fix threshold transfer: calibrate the flag under distance shift, or have it abstain when a variant is further from anything seen.

Decisions for Amit: allow diagnostic design for evaluation (held-out-detection test)? Which labels for the remaining GPU follow-ups, since clinical endpoints are scarce? An external reviewer for the Phase 4 label audit.

sections.title: Also done in Phase 5 and Phase 4 follow-up
body: An in-browser checker on this page scores a pasted Kraken2, Bracken or MetaPhlAn output against the Zymo mocks; the JavaScript was verified against the Python scorer on every committed output.
A Python 3.8 environment for ADAPT was built on the cluster (CPU only, no GPU used). No GPU jobs have been run in Phase 5.

body: scripts/p5_distance_eval.py and scripts/p5_escape_flag.py (both in the repo). Results: data/p5_distance_eval.json, data/p5_escape_flag.json. Run 1, with the linear baseline only, is kept in the repo under results/p5.
